preview_description: Company websites, client portals and web services on Next.js — from structure to launch and support.
title: Website and web app development on Next.js
introtext: I build company websites, client portals and web services end to end: from structure and design to launch and support. You talk directly to the developer, with no account managers and nothing lost in translation. The result is a fast website your team can easily update and that's ready for search from day one.

tasks.title: What clients come to me with

items.title: A new company website from scratch
items.text: A website that explains what you do within a minute, earns trust and brings in leads. That's how the MLS and OcEx websites were made.

items.title: A client portal or web service
items.text: A portal for customers, employees or students: sign-up, documents, requests, statuses and integrations with your systems. Example: the graduate-school portal for IGEM RAS.

items.title: The old website is slow and hard to update
items.text: I move it to a modern stack without losing search rankings. After the move, texts, news and documents are edited in an admin panel — no HTML needed.

items.title: An existing project needs work
items.text: I get to grips with someone else's code, fix bugs, add features, speed things up and take the website on for support.

blocks.title: Structure and prototype
blocks.content: Before any code, I map out the pages and user flows: what people look for, where they click, where they get in touch. Changing decisions at this stage costs the least.

blocks.title: Interface
blocks.content:
Fast loading, mobile-friendly layouts, accessibility. Pages are served with their text already rendered on the server, so Google and AI assistants see all the content straight away.

**Next.js, React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS**

blocks.title: Backend and integrations
blocks.content:
APIs, forms, authentication, payments, CRM, email and third-party services. I choose the architecture to fit the job: a monolith for a website, separate services where load demands it.

**Node.js, REST, GraphQL, PostgreSQL, MySQL, Redis**

blocks.title: An admin panel that's easy to use
blocks.content: Content lives in the Directus headless CMS. Your staff update texts, news, job openings and documents themselves — no developer required.

blocks.title: SEO from day one
blocks.content: Clean URLs, meta tags, schema.org markup, a sitemap, llms.txt for AI assistants and good Core Web Vitals. The website is ready for search as soon as it launches.

blocks.title: Launch and infrastructure
blocks.content:
Server or hosting, HTTPS, CI/CD, backups and monitoring. After launch I hand over all access and a short guide.

**Docker, GitHub Actions, GitLab CI**

sections.title: Why Next.js and not a website builder

blocks.title: Speed
blocks.content: Pages are built ahead of time and stay lightweight. Visitors don't wait, and search engines take speed into account when ranking.

blocks.title: Freedom
blocks.content: No template or pricing-plan limits: any design, any logic, any integration. The code and the data belong to you.

blocks.title: When a builder is the better choice
blocks.content: If you need a simple landing page within a week on a minimal budget, I'll honestly recommend Webflow or Wix. Next.js pays off when a website grows, connects to other systems and needs to bring in customers from search.

steps.title: Intro call
steps.text: We get on a call and go through the task, timeline and budget. If you already have a website, I review it and its analytics.

steps.title: Plan and estimate
steps.text: I send a plan with stages, timelines and cost. We agree on the scope up front, so there are no surprises.

steps.title: Development
steps.text: I work in iterations and show progress on a staging address. You see how it's going and give feedback along the way, not at the very end.

steps.title: Launch
steps.text: I move the website to production, set up analytics and redirects, and show you how to use the admin panel. After that — support, if you need it.

pricing.title: How much a website costs
pricing.note: The total depends on the number of pages and user flows, integrations, and whether design and copy are ready. I give an exact figure after a short brief and fix it before work begins.

plans.title: Company website
plans.text: A corporate or services website: structure, design, development, admin panel and basic SEO.

plans.title: Client portal or web service
plans.text: Authentication, roles, data and document handling, integrations with CRM, payments and external APIs.

plans.title: Improvements
plans.text: New features, bug fixes, performance work, migration to a modern stack.

plans.title: Support
plans.text: Updates, backups, monitoring and small changes on request.

items.question: How much does a turnkey website cost?
items.answer: It depends on the scope: a company website with a few pages and a web service with a client portal differ in effort many times over. The formats above give a rough guide. I name the exact cost after a brief and fix it before we start.

items.question: How long does development take?
items.answer: A company website usually takes one to two months, a web service with a client portal two months or more. What affects the timeline most is how ready the copy is and how quickly decisions get approved.

items.question: Why Next.js and not Webflow, WordPress or Wix?
items.answer: Next.js gives you fast pages, complete freedom in design and logic, and no platform lock-in. For a simple landing page a builder can be the smarter choice — and I'll say so. For a website that grows, works with data and brings in customers from search, Next.js pays off in the long run.

items.question: Will I be able to update the website myself?
items.answer: Yes. I set up Directus — a clear admin panel where you change texts, images, news and documents. No HTML required, and after launch I walk you through how everything works.

items.question: Can I redesign my website without losing search rankings?
items.answer: Yes, if the move is planned in advance. I keep the old URLs or set up 301 redirects, carry over meta tags and copy, and after launch I monitor indexing in Google Search Console.

items.question: Do you take on projects built by someone else?
items.answer: Yes. First I review the code and infrastructure and tell you honestly what shape it's in. Then I suggest a plan: improve it, rewrite it piece by piece, or leave it as it is.
